intro: In the Largo of Dvořák’s New World Symphony, a cor anglais plays the melody over muted strings. Wind chords surround it, and after a section in C♯ minor the string sections reduce to solo players at the quiet return.

sections.label: A · Wind chords modulate to D♭
sections.mNote: Low winds and brass move from E major to D♭.

sections.label: B · Cor anglais solo over muted strings
sections.mNote: The cor anglais melody begins over sustained string chords.

sections.label: C · Flutes and oboes in C♯ minor
sections.mNote: A minor-key tune leads to a measured pizzicato bass.

sections.label: D · Oboe figure in C♯ major
sections.mNote: The oboe begins a dance figure in C♯ major.

sections.label: E · First-movement themes return
sections.mNote: Brass play earlier themes against the Largo melody

sections.label: B′ · Cor anglais theme returns
sections.mNote: The theme returns over four players in each upper string part.

sections.label: A′ · Wind chords, then divided double basses
sections.mNote: The opening chords return; the divided basses end alone.

relations.label: The cor anglais song returns
relations.basis: The large A–B–A′ design restores the opening song after the central minor-key and climactic passages. The later excerpt begins at the return marked near 520 s, not at an inferred instrument entrance. CENS diagonal mean 0.927, sustained 27.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 482.5 s (cache/form/dvorak-9-largo.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening chords, wind and brass
cues.text: Clarinets, bassoons and brass begin with a chain of chords that moves from E major to D♭ major. The violins enter muted, and the wind choir drops out, leaving a single cor anglais.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 73, bars 1–7. The chord sequence is set out in the Dvořák work catalogue: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cor anglais solo, bars 7–10
cues.text: The cor anglais solo in bars 7–10 uses four pitches, F, A♭, E♭ and D♭. Each phrase is in dotted rhythm, played over muted strings.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, movement II, bars 7–10: the opening solo uses those four sounding pitches. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Clarinet sketch and cor anglais
cues.text: In the sketches Dvořák gave the melody to a clarinet, in a more European shape. In the score it is played by the cor anglais, with a stronger pentatonic outline. The instrument’s tone is said to have reminded him of the voice of the singer Harry T. Burleigh.
cues.evidence: Dvořák work catalogue, Symphony No. 9, discussion of the Largo: the original clarinet scoring, the altered melody and the association with Burleigh’s voice. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: Sketchbook inscriptions
cues.text: Dvořák wrote two phrases into his sketches for this movement: “Legend” and “The Legend Begins”. Michael Beckerman heard the opening chords as a musical “once upon a time”. The sketchbooks contain earlier versions of these chords, one of which begins and ends in C major.
cues.evidence: Dvořák work catalogue, Symphony No. 9: the sketchbook inscriptions, the surviving variants of the opening chords and Beckerman’s reading. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: William Arms Fisher, Goin’ Home, 1922
cues.text: In the summer of 1922 William Arms Fisher, a former pupil of the composer, played a piano arrangement of the Largo and began to write words to it. He made the cor anglais melody into the song Goin’ Home, nearly thirty years after the symphony.
cues.evidence: Fisher’s account of composing the words in summer 1922 is quoted in the performance-history section of the work catalogue: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/.

cues.title: Letter to Oskar Nedbal, 1900
cues.text: In February 1900 Dvořák sent Oskar Nedbal, who was preparing to conduct the symphony in Berlin, a published analysis of it. He asked him to leave out “that nonsense about my using Indian and American motifs – it is a lie!” He had meant only to write in the spirit of American national melodies.
cues.evidence: Dvořák to Oskar Nedbal, February 1900, in the English translation given in the Dvořák work catalogue, “sources of inspiration”: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: Middle section in C♯ minor
cues.text: The key changes from D♭ major to C♯ minor, on the same sounding tonic. Flutes and oboes share a new tune over repeated string chords. Later, pizzicato bass notes give this middle section the tread of a funeral march.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 78, Un poco più mosso, and the ensuing pizzicato passage. The minor section and march are described in the Dvořák work catalogue.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Indian melodies, New York Herald, 1893
cues.text: Dvořák told the New York Herald in December 1893 that he had “carefully studied a certain number of Indian melodies which a friend gave me”. Iroquois performers had sung and danced in Prague for ten days in August 1879. He saw Buffalo Bill’s Wild West show in spring 1894, after the symphony was finished.
cues.evidence: Dvořák work catalogue, “sources of inspiration”: the New York Herald interview of 15 December 1893, the Iroquois visit to Prague in August 1879, and David Beveridge’s 2022 research on the date of the Buffalo Bill visit. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: Public rehearsal, Carnegie Hall, 1893
cues.text: On 15 December 1893 people queued in heavy rain for the public rehearsal at Carnegie Hall, and every seat was sold. Anton Seidl conducted the New York Philharmonic. The official première followed the next evening.
cues.evidence: The première section of the Dvořák work catalogue describes the rain, queue, sold-out public rehearsal and concert: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/.

cues.title: Oboe solo, C♯-major episode
cues.text: A quick figure for solo oboe divides the long phrases into short groups of notes. Flutes and clarinets join with trills and runs. The harmony moves to C♯ major, and the strings play a crescendo underneath.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 84, rehearsal 4: solo oboe, then flute and clarinet figures above a string crescendo. The C♯-major episode is identified in the work catalogue.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Climax with first-movement themes
cues.text: The dance builds to a full orchestral climax. The first movement’s main theme and closing theme return alongside the Largo theme, with the brass above the strings.
cues.evidence: The work catalogue identifies the Largo theme, the first movement’s main theme and its closing theme in this climax: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/. Šourek score, printed pp. 85–88.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the cor anglais theme
cues.text: At Meno mosso, Tempo I the opening tempo returns. The cor anglais plays the theme again in D♭ major, accompanied by four players in each violin, viola and cello part.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 88, rehearsal 5: returning cor anglais, five-flat signature and four players in each upper string part.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Strings reduced to soloists
cues.text: The string parts are reduced again, to two players each and then to solo violin, viola, cello and bass. Fermatas separate the phrases.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 89, bars 105–110: two players per string part, fermatas and subsequent solo markings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Applause after the Largo, 1893
cues.text: At the première on 16 December 1893, the audience would not allow the concert to continue after the Largo until Dvořák appeared and bowed. His son Otakar, who was in the hall, recorded this in his memoirs.
cues.evidence: Otakar Dvořák’s memoirs, quoted in the première section of the Dvořák work catalogue: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: Return of the wind chords
cues.text: Bassoons, horns, trombones and tuba bring back the introductory chords, which move slowly to D♭ major once more. After the last wind chord, divided double basses descend and the movement ends.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 91–92, bars 120–127: return of the wind chords and final divided double basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Wind chords to cor anglais
transitions.from: A · Wind chords modulate to D♭
transitions.to: B · Cor anglais solo over muted strings
transitions.how: The wind chords move from E major to D♭. Their final G♭-minor chord resolves onto D♭ major, a minor-subdominant plagal cadence. Muted strings take over the held harmony, and the cor anglais begins its tune above them. The double basses hold D♭.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 73, bars 1–7; the chord succession is given at https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/.

transitions.title: D♭ major to C♯ minor
transitions.from: B · Cor anglais solo over muted strings
transitions.to: C · Flutes and oboes in C♯ minor
transitions.how: The song ends, and D♭ is respelt as C♯. E♮ replaces F as the third above it, so the harmony turns to the minor. At Un poco più mosso (bar 46), flutes and oboes play the new tune together over repeated chords in the second violins and violas.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 77–78, leading into bar 46, Un poco più mosso.

transitions.title: Solo oboe introduces the quicker figure
transitions.from: C · Flutes and oboes in C♯ minor
transitions.to: D · Oboe figure in C♯ major
transitions.how: The strings, in the minor, play more softly and settle on a held C♯. A solo oboe then plays a quick figure above them, and flutes and clarinets follow with trills and running notes. The tonic remains C♯, now with the major third E♯, and the episode is a quasi-scherzo in C♯ major (Šourek full score, printed p. 84, rehearsal 4).
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 84, rehearsal 4. The work catalogue identifies the episode as a quasi-scherzo in C♯ major.

transitions.title: Brass brings back first-movement themes
transitions.from: D · Oboe figure in C♯ major
transitions.how: The strings make a crescendo beneath the quick wind figures. Brass and timpani join, and the main and closing themes of the first movement sound against the Largo melody, so that three melodies are heard together.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 85–88. The combination of the Largo melody with the first movement’s main and closing themes is described in the Dvořák work catalogue.

transitions.title: Four strings to a part
transitions.how: The orchestra slows and softens into Meno mosso, Tempo I, the original tempo, at rehearsal 5. The cor anglais returns with the D♭-major melody over four players in each upper string part. The brass and timpani play their last quiet punctuation and then stop, leaving the melody to the cor anglais and strings.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 88, rehearsal 5: original tempo, D♭-major return and reduced string numbers.

transitions.title: Return of the introductory wind chords
transitions.to: A′ · Wind chords, then divided double basses
transitions.how: The solo violin’s last phrase falls to ppp. At bar 120 bassoons, horns, trombones and tuba play the opening chord sequence again, which moves once more towards D♭ major. The bass changes with each chord, and the divided double basses play the final bars.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 91–92, the return of the introductory chords at bar 120 and final bass writing.

source.title: Dvořák, Symphony No. 9, II. Largo, full score (Otakar Šourek edition)
source.locator: Printed pp. 73–92, bars 1–127: cor anglais over muted strings, the C♯-minor middle, quick wind figures and reduced strings at the return. The tuba plays in the opening and closing chords; its rests are confirmed in the Breitkopf part, https://www.imslp.eu/files/imglnks/euimg/5/59/IMSLP726228-PMLP8710-Dvorak-Symph9-29-ta.pdf.

timeline.note: Clarinets, bassoons and brass move through a sequence of chords; timpani mark the arrival in D♭ before muted strings enter.
The cor anglais plays above muted strings; clarinet figures move beneath the later phrases.
Woodwind phrases build to a brief brass chord, and the strings then resume the melody.
First violins take the melody, then pass it back to the cor anglais above quietly held strings.
Flutes and oboes play together in C♯ minor above repeated chords in the second violins and violas.
Oboe and clarinet answer the violins, while the low strings play pizzicato underneath.
Short woodwind phrases continue above the quiet strings as the C♯-minor section dies away.
A short solo oboe figure passes to the flutes and clarinets, and the strings play a crescendo under their trills and runs.
The brass play the first movement’s themes against the Largo melody, with timpani beneath the full strings and winds.
The cor anglais returns over four players in each violin, viola and cello part.
The strings reduce to two players in each part, then to solos, with rests between the phrases.
Bassoons, horns, trombones and tuba repeat the opening chords; the strings rise towards the last cadence.
The wind play a last chord, and the divided double basses finish alone.

composer.epithet: Composer of the Slavonic Dances, who played viola in an opera orchestra for nine years before his music became widely known.
facts: Violist at Prague’s Provisional Theatre, 1862–71; organist and piano teacher
Prague Conservatory; director of New York’s National Conservatory, 1892–95
Nine symphonies; operas, concertos, chamber music, choral works and songs
composer.background:
In the village band at Nelahozeves, north of Prague, the musicians collected their money by stopping a couple halfway through a dance and asking them to pay. Young Antonín Dvořák handed his share straight to his father, the village butcher and innkeeper. “I belonged to ours as soon as I could fiddle a little,” he told the London Sunday Times on 10 May 1885. He was born in Nelahozeves on 8 September 1841.

At Zlonice, the schoolteacher Antonín Liehmann taught him harmony and several instruments. Dvořák remembered bringing home a polka for the band to try. The opening chord came out all right except for the cornet, whose part he had written in the wrong key. In 1857 he went to the Prague Organ School, graduating two years later. He played viola in a dance band which became the nucleus of the Provisional Theatre orchestra in 1862. For nine years he sat in the pit, often under Smetana, playing operas while writing his own music at home.
